Every state has its own FWC. These are the official state agencies for this region — registration, boating laws, fishing licenses and state-run launch lists, straight from the source. The state sites carry the official rules.

Maine Dept. of Inland Fisheries & Wildlife

Maine's FWC — fishing, boat registration and boating laws in one department. Public launches are run by the Bureau of Parks & Lands.

Register a boat
Boating: registration & laws — MDIFWHow to register, fees, and Maine's boating laws and boater education.
Public launches
State public boat launch list — Bureau of Parks & LandsThe state's own ramp list — the same list this region's ramps were built from.
Fishing
Licenses & rules — MDIFWFishing licenses and rules live with the same department.
NH Fish & Game Dept. + NH Marine Patrol

New Hampshire splits the job: Fish & Game runs fishing and the state's public boat access sites; the Marine Patrol (State Police) runs boating laws and safety certificates. Boat registration is issued by the Dept. of Safety / DMV.

Boating & access
Boating and Access — NH Fish & GameThe Statewide Public Boat Access Program — 140+ state access sites.
Laws & safety
Marine Patrol — NH State PoliceBoating laws, enforcement, and the safety certificate required to run a motorboat over 25 hp.
Fishing
Licenses & rules — NH Fish & GameFishing licenses and rules live with Fish & Game.
Vermont Fish & Wildlife Dept.

Vermont's FWC — it also maintains 180+ developed fishing access areas across the state. Boat registration paperwork runs through the Vermont DMV.

Boating
Boating in Vermont — VT Fish & WildlifeSafety course (required if you were born after Jan. 1, 1974), registration info, and the boating handbook.
Public access
Fishing access areas — VT Fish & WildlifeThe state's own access-area program — ramps and shore fishing statewide.
MA Environmental Police + MassWildlife

Massachusetts splits it too: the Environmental Police handle boat registration, titling and boating-law enforcement; MassWildlife handles fishing.

Register a boat
Boat Registration — MA Environmental PoliceRegistration, titling and renewals. Note: a boater safety-certificate rule for all motorboat operators takes effect April 1, 2026.
Fishing
MassWildlifeFishing licenses, rules, and the state's wildlife lands and access points.
Connecticut DEEP

Connecticut's FWC is the Dept. of Energy & Environmental Protection — its Boating Division runs laws, safety and state launches; vessels themselves register with the DMV.

Boating
Boating and Paddling — CT DEEPBoating laws, state boat launches, and the annual Connecticut Boater's Guide.
Register a boat
Boat Registration — CT DEEPWhat has to be registered and how the DMV registration works.
Fishing
Fisheries Licenses and Permits — CT DEEPFishing licenses and permits from DEEP's Fisheries Division.
Rhode Island DEM

Rhode Island's FWC is the Dept. of Environmental Management — it runs boat registration itself, plus Fish & Wildlife and Marine Fisheries.

Register a boat
Boat Registration — RI DEMDEM's Office of Boat Registration & Licensing; renewals run online through Rhode Island Outdoors.
Fishing
Licenses — RI DEM (Rhode Island Outdoors)Freshwater and saltwater fishing licenses and rules.

New England Fishing

Tautog season is the main event from Buzzards Bay to Long Island Sound, with the last stripers of the fall run mixed in. What's actually biting this week, from this week's reports.

Weekly Report — Wednesday, November 4, 2026

Today's Best Bets

1. Tautog — The consensus No. 1 fish in southern New England right now. Buzzards Bay is producing around 50 feet of water (fish to 24 inches this week), Boston Harbor anglers are picking them off the pilings at Long Wharf, Rhode Island rock piles are giving up fish in about 50 feet in the bay and on deep drops near 75 feet, and Connecticut's bite is on shallow rock in 25 feet or less. Green crabs are the bait — white crabs on the deep Rhode Island drops — on rigs in deep water, 1–3 oz jigs in the shallows.
2. Striped bass — The fall run is thinning but not done. Massachusetts feeds have been patchy — Quincy Bay and the Weymouth Back River, stragglers at Plum Island's Lot 6, and holdovers chasing herring fry in the Charles and Mystic rivers. Rhode Island's Providence and Seekonk Rivers and the South County breachways are still holding fish, and Connecticut's eastern Sound had surface blitzes with more bass staging at the Thames, Connecticut and Housatonic mouths. Topwaters and big soft-plastic plugs by day; eel imitators after dark.
3. Black sea bass (Rhode Island & Connecticut only) — Still open in Rhode Island and Connecticut — Massachusetts' season closed Oct. 14, so this is a RI/CT bet only. They're mixing with tautog and scup on the rock piles out of Point Judith and on Niantic party boats. Small jigs, or rigs baited with squid or clam.
Note: Also around: jumbo bluefish at The Race, extra-large scup with easy limits, a few late false albacore and bonito from Niantic to Groton and in Vineyard Sound, mackerel stacked in Boston Harbor, and a night bluefin bite on Stellwagen Bank on staggered live squid. Nothing solid came in from New Hampshire or Maine this week — this card is southern New England sourced, and it says so.

Tide windows: Boston: high 6:55 AM (9.5 ft) and 7:18 PM (9.6 ft), low 12:59 PM. Fish the moving water around the highs — Massachusetts reports say a moving tide is the trigger for the tog bite.
Bait: Green crabs are the tog bait everywhere (white crabs on Rhode Island's deep drops); live eels after dark for holdover stripers. Find a bait shop near the ramp · Check today's tides & forecast.
Compiled from On The Water's Oct. 29 reports (Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island), The Fisherman, and the MA DMF, CT DEEP and RI DEM rules pages (full source list in the preview folder) — general areas only, no secret spots burned. Curated roundup from public sources and seasonal patterns.
November

What's Biting Now

• Tautog — Buzzards Bay around 50 ft, Boston Harbor pilings, Rhode Island rock piles, Connecticut shallow rock; green crabs.
• Striped bass — Providence & Seekonk Rivers, South County breachways, eastern Sound blitzes, river-mouth staging.
• Black sea bass — Rhode Island & Connecticut rock piles only (Massachusetts season closed Oct. 14).
• Scup — extra-large fish, easy limits, mixed right in with the tog.
• Bluefish — jumbos at The Race; false albacore and bonito tailing off from Niantic to Groton.
Don't forget

Licenses & Seasons

• Striped bass: 28″ to under 31″, 1 per day, open year-round in MA/CT/RI; inline circle hooks required when fishing natural bait.
• Tautog: MA Oct. 15–Dec. 31 — 5 fish, 16″ min, only 1 over 21″, 10 per vessel. RI the same dates and limits per RI's official guide. CT Oct. 10–Nov. 28 only — 3 fish, 16″ min. Know whose water you're in.
• Black sea bass: CT May 16–Nov. 25, 15.5″ min, 4 fish (private boat). RI May 16–Dec. 31, 16″ min, 3 fish. MA closed since Oct. 14.
• Bonito / false albacore (MA): 16″ min, 5 combined per day.
• Licenses: a saltwater license or registry is required in each state — check CT DEEP and RI DEM before you go; MA DMF posts the full set of marine rules.

New to Boating

New to boating? The 8 steps below, in the right order. No experience assumed.

1Get legal first

Every New England state has its own boater-education rule, and they genuinely differ: Maine and New Hampshire tie the course/certificate to boats over 25 hp, Vermont requires a card for operators born after Jan. 1, 1974, Rhode Island requires a certificate for boats over 10 hp and for every PWC operator, Connecticut requires its Safe Boating Certificate, and Massachusetts is phasing a certificate in for everyone by April 1, 2028. Check your state's exact rule first — tap through to State Rules & Agencies for each state's official links.

→ 2Gear up: the safety checklist

Life jackets for everyone, throwable cushion, fire extinguisher, flares, horn, kill-switch lanyard. See exactly what the Coast Guard requires.

→ 3Rent before you buy

Try different boats through rentals or a boat club before spending a dollar. Learn what you actually like on the water first.

→ 4Learn the markers

“Red, right, returning” — channel markers, no-wake signs, and who has the right of way. The rules that keep everyone safe.

→ 5Launch, dock & anchor

Ramp etiquette, docking without the drama, knots that hold, and anchoring that actually sticks.

→ 6Respect New England waters

Cold water is the big one: the Coast Guard counts any water at 70°F or below as cold water, and New England water stays cold well into summer — dress for the water, not the air, and wear the life jacket. Add some of the biggest tides on the East Coast, growing toward the Bay of Fundy, where NOAA puts the rise and fall at as much as 53 feet; fog that can roll in and cut visibility to almost nothing; and lobster-pot buoys whose lines can foul a prop or rudder. Local knowledge that saves props — and lives.

→ 7Before every trip

Check the marine forecast, tell someone your float plan, and monitor VHF channel 16. If the bay looks angry, stay at the dock.

→ 8Act like you've been here before

Boating etiquette — the ramp rules, guest rules, and sandbar manners that keep the regulars friendly and get you invited back.

→
Beginner mistakes that cost money

Running aground on a falling tide · getting caught out when the fog rolls in · boating with no tow coverage · buying the wrong boat before ever renting one.
